title: Ryoma Brokers the Satsuma-Choshu Alliance
text:
In the 1860s two powerful southwestern domains of Japan, Satsuma and Choshu, both wanted to change a shogunate that seemed helpless before the Western powers. But they hated each other. In 1864 Satsuma troops had helped drive Choshu forces out of Kyoto in bloody fighting, and Choshu men wore sandals with the word Satsuma written on them so they could tread on it.

Sakamoto Ryoma, a former samurai of the Tosa domain who had left his lord to work for national reform, saw that neither domain could defeat the shogunate alone. With his ally Nakaoka Shintaro he worked to bring them together. He found a practical first step: Choshu, under threat of attack by the shogunate, could not buy modern weapons openly, so Ryoma's trading company arranged for Western rifles and a ship to be bought in Satsuma's name and passed on to Choshu.

In March 1866 (the first month of the old Japanese calendar), in Kyoto, Ryoma brought together Saigo Takamori of Satsuma and Kido Takayoshi of Choshu. For days both sides waited for the other to propose terms first, out of pride. Ryoma confronted Saigo, and an agreement was reached. Kido wrote out its six points and asked Ryoma to endorse it, which Ryoma did on the back of the document.

That summer Choshu defeated the shogunate's punitive expedition. In 1868 Satsuma and Choshu forces led the coup and war that restored imperial rule. Ryoma did not see it: he was assassinated in Kyoto in December 1867.
lesson: Former enemies can become the most powerful partners when they share a larger goal. A trusted go-between and a practical first step can break a deadlock of pride.
people: Sakamoto Ryoma, Saigo Takamori, Kido Takayoshi, Nakaoka Shintaro
source: Marius Jansen, Sakamoto Ryoma and the Meiji Restoration (1961)
caveat: Some details, including the sandals and Ryoma's confrontation with Saigo, come from later traditional accounts.
